explain.say: In 1854 the doctor John Snow traced a deadly cholera outbreak in London to one water pump on Broad Street. Since then, engineers have learned to make even a muddy river safe to drink. They do it in a row of steps called a treatment train. Here it is on the board, river on the left, your tap on the right.

explain.say: Now the real thing in 3D: a water treatment works. Follow the water from the intake through mixing, flocculation, the settling tank, the sand filter and chlorination to the clear water tank. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: The drinking water treatment train: from muddy river to safe tap water

explain.say: Look at the second stage, coagulation. River water is cloudy because of tiny clay bits, each carrying a negative charge, so they push each other apart and never sink. A dose of alum, aluminium sulphate, cancels that charge. At twenty milligrams per litre, a works treating fifteen million litres a day uses three hundred kilograms of alum daily.

explain.say: Now see the cloudiness, called turbidity, fall. Slow paddles help the clay bits clump into fluffy flocs, which sink in the settling tank. Fifty turbidity units in the river drop to about five after settling, and below one after the sand filters. Which stage do you think removes the most dirt?

draw.text: Turbidity is measured in NTU: how much light the water scatters.

explain.say: Settling does the heavy lifting! Clean-looking water can still carry germs, so the last big step is disinfection, shown lighting up now. Chlorine kills bacteria and viruses, and a small amount stays in the pipes to guard the water all the way to you. How big must the works be? A town of a hundred thousand people using a hundred and fifty litres each needs fifteen million litres a day.

explain.say: Each stage is a barrier, so if one slips the others still protect you. Engineers call this the multiple barrier approach. Lovely work! Exam tip: always list the stages in order and say what each one removes. Challenge: why must coagulation come before the filters, not after?

faq.q: What is a water treatment train?
faq.a: It is the sequence of processes that turns raw water into drinking water: screening, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration and disinfection, then storage and supply.

faq.q: What does coagulation do in water treatment?
faq.a: Coagulation adds a chemical such as alum or ferric chloride that cancels the negative charge on tiny clay and colour particles, so they can stick together into flocs that settle.

faq.q: Why is chlorine added to drinking water?
faq.a: Chlorine kills bacteria and viruses, and a small residual stays in the pipes to protect the water on its way to the tap. The WHO guideline maximum is 5 milligrams per litre.

faq.q: How much water does a town need each day?
faq.a: Multiply the population by the daily use per person. A town of 100,000 people at 150 litres each needs 15 million litres, or 15,000 cubic metres, a day, plus extra for leaks and peaks.
Turbidity is the cloudiness of water, measured in NTU by how much light it scatters. Drinking water should be below 1 NTU, and ideally much lower, so disinfection works well.

facts: Jersey City in the USA began continuous chlorination of a public water supply in 1908, one of the first large systems to do so.
The WHO guideline value for chlorine in drinking water is 5 mg/L, well above the amount normally used.
James Simpson built a slow sand filter for London's Chelsea Waterworks in 1829.

quiz.say: A town of 50,000 people uses 200 litres per person per day. What is the daily demand?
quiz.show: A town of 50,000 people uses 200 L per person per day. Daily demand?

options.say: ten thousand cubic metres a day
one thousand cubic metres a day
a hundred thousand cubic metres a day

quiz.why: 50,000 × 200 L = 10,000,000 L, and 1 cubic metre is 1,000 L, so 10,000 m³ per day.

wrong.1: That slips a factor of ten when changing litres to cubic metres.
wrong.2: That multiplies instead of dividing by 1,000.

quiz.say: Which stage removes most of the flocs?
quiz.show: Which stage removes most of the flocs?
quiz.why: In the calm settling tank the heavy flocs sink to the bottom as sludge.

wrong.1: Disinfection kills germs; it does not remove particles.
wrong.2: Screens only stop large objects like leaves and fish.
